background.definition: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common type of skin malignancy. It is typically slow growing and locally invasive with low malignancy potential; however, significant disfigurement can occur if left untreated. It occurs most often on sun-exposed areas and occasionally may be found on sun-protected skin.

list.listitem: The age-adjusted incidence of BCC is 99.6 per 100,000 women (95% CI, 80.4-118.7) and 191.0 per 100,000 men (156.9-225.0).
BCC is mostly seen in the elderly, but incidence in younger patients is increasing.
The estimated lifetime risk in the white population is 28% to 33%.
Increased ultraviolet (UV) exposure.
Patients with xeroderma pigmentosum, basal cell nevus syndrome (Gorlin syndrome), Bazex-Dupré-Christol syndrome, and oculocutaneous albinism are at increased risk.
Outdoor workers are at greater risk (OR 1.4).

Other risk factors include blonde or fair hair, light skin color, exposure to arsenic, coal tar, or ionizing radiation, immunosuppression such as organ transplantation, and UV light exposure including tanning beds.
The risk of BCC is increased with increasing numbers of nevi on an extremity.
Thought to arise from basal or follicular level pluripotential cells.
UV light is the most common etiologic factor that can induce DNA mutations.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Prior history of squamous cell carcinoma

list.listitem: Recommend sun protection (sunscreen, hats, long-sleeved clothing, and avoiding the midday sun) beginning at a very early age because much sun damage occurs in childhood. Counseling of young women in particular has been shown to decrease risky sun behavior, especially if focused on appearance more than health benefits. B
Avoid tanning (natural and artificial) and sunburn especially in children. B
The US Preventive Services Task Force finds insufficient evidence to recommend for or against routine counseling by primary care clinicians to prevent skin cancer. B
Regular application of sunscreen has prolonged preventive benefits for squamous cell carcinoma, but has no clear benefit in reducing BCC. B

In those with a history of keratinocyte cancer, small trials suggest possible benefit to oral nicotinamide, celecoxib, and difluoromethylornithine (DFMO) in reducing the risk for BCC but no benefit to oral and topical retinoids or dietary supplementation with selenium or beta-carotene. B
Diagnosis begins with a history of a growing, ulcerating, or bleeding lesion typically in a sun-exposed area. C
Look for clinical features that are suspicious for different subtypes of BCC including nodular (pearly with telangiectasias), superficial (scaling and thready border), and sclerosing (scarlike). C
Dermoscopy can be used as an adjunct in identification but the final diagnosis is based on histology. C
Biopsy suspicious lesions with a shave, punch, or excisional biopsy. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Scaly, erythematous papule; may be similar in appearance to BCC; risk of metastasis
Typically in elderly white patient on chronically sun-exposed areas; feels rough; macule
Yellowish soft papules typically found where sebaceous glands are located (face, chest, areola, vulva)
Occur as a small firm, pink or skin-colored papule most often seen on the nose
Occurs on sun-exposed areas as firm, rounded, skin-colored or slightly pinkish red that may have central ulcerated area with keratin plug
Great variability in size and pigmentation of lesions
Sharply defined "stuck-on" verrucous appearance with variation in color
Pearly papules or nodules found on the nose and face that are best diagnosed by biopsy; benign

list.listitem: Suspicious lesions by history are those lesions that are growing, ulcerating, or bleeding without provocation in sun-exposed areas. A persistent skin ulcer on the face is a skin cancer until proven otherwise.

All types of BCCs are seen most often in sun-exposed areas with the majority being on the face and neck. Nodular BCCs: raised pearly pink, smooth translucent surface with telangiectasias; may be pigmented or ulcerated. Superficial BCCs: red or pink scaling thin papules or plaques. Sclerosing BCC: ivory, skin-colored, or pink, flat or atrophic, indurated, may resemble scars.
The risk of BCC is increased with increasing numbers of nevi on an extremity.

Biopsy is necessary to confirm diagnosis. Shave biopsy with #15 blade or razor blade is the easiest method to obtain tissue for pathology in a suspected BCC. Shave biopsy can be used for other types of BCCs, but a scoop shave approach is needed if the lesion is flat.

Punch biopsy can be done to obtain specimen from flat lesions and if there is concern for a deeper process. Biopsy the area that is most suspicious and be aware that sampling error can occur. A negative biopsy of a suspicious lesion should be followed up with another biopsy or full excisional biopsy may be utilized.
Excisional biopsy is rarely utilized to obtain tissue as the initial procedure for histopathologic diagnosis.

With dermoscopy, nonpigmented superficial BCC displays dermoscopic features of shiny white to pink milky areas with short-branching telangiectasias. Pigmentation in the shape of maple leaves may be seen in pigmented BCCs.

Dermoscopy showed sensitivity and specificity of 91% and 95% respectively for diagnosis of BCC in a meta-analysis of 17 studies. Adding dermoscopy to naked eye examination significantly improved sensitivity from 67% to 85% and specificity from 97% to 98%. The accuracy was higher for pigmented BCCs, and sensitivity increased when dermoscopy was performed by experts.

Optical coherence tomography improved sensitivity and specificity when compared with visual inspection plus dermoscopy; reflectance confocal microscopy has also been shown to have high diagnostic value. B
A biopsy is required any time there is a lesion suspicious for BCC or any other type of skin cancer.
The final diagnosis is always based on histology. Shave biopsy is generally used for nodular lesions, and punch or excisional biopsy is used for flat lesions.

Lesions should be stratified as low or high risk of recurrence based on clinical and pathologic features. Features indicating a higher risk of recurrence include high-risk locations such as the face, size, poorly defined borders, within a prior irradiated site, and aggressive histologic morphologies including morpheaform pattern.
Factors to consider in choosing treatment are the location of the lesion, lesion size, histologic type, age of patient, comorbid conditions, and cost. A
Surgical excision of the entire lesion has higher cure rates than cryosurgery or curettage and electrodesiccation; consider the latter for low-risk tumors in low-risk anatomic areas. A

Mohs micrographic surgery has the lowest recurrence rates. It should be reserved for high-risk BCC, larger lesions, recurrent lesions, and those where tissue sparing is a priority (such as facial lesions). A
Imiquimod cream is a safe and effective treatment for superficial BCC (87% treatment response for superficial BCC and 76% for nodular BCC); 5-FU is also an option for topical therapy. A

Nonsurgical treatments e.g. imiquimod, photodynamic therapy, and 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) can be considered for low-risk superficial basal cell carcinomas in patients who decline surgery or in whom surgery is not feasible.A

Imiquimod cream applied 5 times a week is a safe and effective treatment for superficial BCC.It is possible to achieve an 87% to 88% treatment response for superficial BCC using a once-daily regimen for 6 weeks and a 76% treatment response when treating nodular BCC for 12 weeks.

A non-inferiority randomized controlled study for superficial and nodular BCC compared imiquimod 5% cream or surgical excision with primary outcome of clinical resolution of the cancer at time of initial treatment and absence of recurrence at 3 year follow-up. Of 501 patients, 401 contributed to intention to treat analyses at year 3 and 383 (96%) had data at year 5 with imiquimod success rates (82.5%) compared with 97.7% for surgery (p < 0.001). These figures were comparable to year 3 at 83.6% for imiquimod and 98.4% for surgery respectively. Most imiquimod failures occurred in year 1.

5-year results of a prospective non-inferiority randomized controlled trial comparing effectiveness of PDT, imiquimod and topical 5-FU in superficial BCC showed 5% imiquimod as superior to both PDT and 5-FU for efficacy. 601 patients were analyzed for intention to treat results showing tumor free survival for PDT of 62.7% (95% CI 55.3-69.2), 80.5% (95% CI 74-85.6) for imiquimod and 70% for 5-FU (95% CI 62.9-76).

A meta-analysis of 13 RCTs with 4256 patients showed that imiquimod 5% was associated with a significantly higher histological clearance rate and composite clearance rate. However, more patients with imiquimod developed adverse events than those with other treatments.
5-fluorouracil cream applied twice daily for 3 to 6 weeks is also an effective treatment. It has also been studied as an intralesional injection.,

A review identified largely case reports and small case series of intralesional chemotherapy for BCC. The greatest experience and success appeared to be with intralesional 5-FU, bleomycin, and interferon.
Factors to consider in choosing treatment are the location of the lesion, lesion size, histologic type, age of patient, comorbid conditions, and cost. A

Surgical excision of the entire lesion has higher cure rates than cryosurgery or curettage and electrodesiccation (C&E).Recurrence rates are low, especially on the trunk and extremities. A 4 mm margin is recommended.
Mohs micrographic surgery has the lowest recurrence rates (3.2%-6.7%). It should be reserved for larger lesions and those where tissue sparing is a priority (such as facial lesions).

A study of patients with BCC (n=287) treated with MOHS of whom 68% had residual histologic tumor. It was more likely in men, in high risk sites, with smaller biopsy sizes, and larger preoperative size tumors.
C&E using 3 cycles and cryotherapy using a freeze-thaw-freeze cycle may be considered if other more effective treatments are not feasible. B

A systematic review summarized the evidence for a variety of surgical techniques in the treatment of BCC:
Mohs micrographic surgery (3 studies, N = 2660): mean strict recurrence rate 1.1% (21/1989). Surgical excision (3 studies, N = 1303): strict recurrence rate was 8.1% in one study; mean cumulative 5-year rate (all 3 studies) was 5.3. % Cryosurgery (4 studies, N = 796): mean strict recurrence rate 4.3% (24/556); cumulative 5-year rate (3 studies) ranged from 0 to 16%. Curettage and desiccation (6 studies, N = 4212): strict recurrence rate was given in one study as 8.5%; cumulative 5-year rate ranged from 5.7% to 18.8%.

A study followed 89 patients with 280 BCCs who opted for watchful waiting without treatment, largely due to advanced age or frailty. Median follow-up was 9 months. The estimated increase in size was 4.5 mm for BCCs containing an infiltrative or micronodular component, but only 1 mm for those without such a component.
In persons with a previous nonmelanoma skin cancer, treatment with beta-carotene did not reduce the incidence of new skin cancers over a 5-year period of treatment and observation.

Photodynamic therapy is a treatment option for basal cell carcinoma. A clinical trial randomized 162 patients to conventional methyl aminolevulinate (MAL) photodynamic therapy or 5-aminoalevulinic acid (ALA) photodynamic therapy for treatment of superficial BCC. At one year follow-up, the likelihood of remaining free from treatment failure was 92.3% with ALA and 83.4% with MAL, p = 0.091.

A systematic review of 15 randomized trials with 2327 patients concluded that the 5 year sustained clearance of photodynamic therapy is good but is lower than that for excisional surgery (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.63-0.91) as well as imiquimod (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.71-0.95).
For non-surgical candidates, primary radiation therapy can be an effective treatment option in the appropriately selected patient. Laser therapy is not recommended.
Refer for Mohs surgery tumors that are recurrent, large, aggressive, or in cosmetically or functionally important areas.
Large tumors invading the head and neck may be referred for surgery in the operating room (under general anesthetic).

Multidisciplinary consultation and hedgehog pathway inhibitors are recommended for patients with metastatic BCC; oral vismodegib and sonidegib have been approved by the US FDA as the first systemic therapy for metastatic BCC.
Wound infection is a potential complication of surgical excision or biopsy. Inform patients of the signs and symptoms of wound infections and provide follow-up as needed.
Untreated lesions can gradually grow and become a significant cause of disfigurement and morbidity. Metastases are rare, and mostly occur at the head and neck. C
The 3-year risk of recurrence after having a single BCC is 44% for a new BCC and 6% for a new squamous cell carcinoma. B
After diagnosis of a first BCC, follow-up for new skin cancers should be performed on at least an annual basis. C

A study followed 89 patients with 280 BCCs who opted for watchful waiting without treatment, largely due to advanced age or frailty. Median follow-up was 9 months. The estimated increase in size was 4.5 mm for BCCs containing an infiltrative or micronodular component, but only 1 mm for those without such a component.
A study of the entire population of iceland found that BCC is not associated with worse survival, assuming it is appropriately treated.
